newsitem.title: USA: Miami Commission expects to pass fire-rescue fee.
newsitem.headline: Miami Commission expects to pass fire-rescue fee.

text.p: The Miami City Commission inched closer Monday to adopting a $24 million fire-rescue district fee, the final component in the five-year budget it must submit to a state oversight board by Tuesday.

City Manager Ed Marquez proposed replacing the yearly fee of $166 for garbage collection with an annnual fire-rescue fee that would start at $166 for single-family homes and rise according to square footage.
Unlike the garbage fee, the fire-rescue fee would also be levied on tax-exempt property owned by the Dade County government, the county school board and non-profit institutions.
As originally proposed, it would have raised $30 million annually, or about $13 million above the cost of services. The surplus would go into the city's general fund, offsetting other fixed costs.

At a meeting Monday morning, the five city commissioners grudgingly said they could approve the fee if it was reduced by $6 million or about 20 percent. They proposed offsetting that with $6 million of additional cuts in capital projects, recyling services and other programs.
The commission sent Marquez and finance department officials back to rework the proposal and planned to reconvene at 5 p.m. Monday for final discussions and a vote.
Commissioners have been loathe to impose the fee, but said Monday it was the only way to raise enough recurring new revenues to balance the budget.
"We all know the fire fee is wrong. It's the wrong way to go about this but it is the only optioin," Commissioner Tomas Regalado said.
Mayor Joe Carollo, one of the five commissioners, said the city may be able to further reduce the fee by making other budget cuts before the fee takes effect in January.
"We still have the option to revisit any changes that need to be made," he said.
After several city officials resigned in a corruption scandal last fall, the city discovered a $68 million deficit in its $275 million budget for the year that began Oct, 1, 1996.

Gov. Lawton Chiles appointed a financial oversight board to guide the city's recovery, with the understanding that Chiles could take control of the city if the commisison fails to correct recurring budget shortages.

The city balanced its 1997 budget, using employee concessions, cuts in services and one-time revenues such as proceeds from land sales. The oversight board set a Tuesday deadline for the city to submit a balanced budget through 2001.
Carollo said he was confident that at least the first two years of the budget would meet the oversight board's requirement that recurring costs be met with recurring revenues.
"I think for the next fiscal year (1998), they will accept it. There might be some give and take in the next three years," Carollo said.
